extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (especially philosophy of religion and epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical chapter arguing that although the Absolute (the Unconditioned) is inconceivable in content, consciousness compels belief in its positive existence; it sets out the proper functions and failings of Religion and Science and explains how their mutual correction leads to reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of persistence as measure of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only possible measure of relative validity among our beliefs, is the degree of their persistence in opposition to the efforts made to change them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beliefs that persist under repeated attempts to negate or alter them have higher epistemic warrant. The text uses the indestructible, ever-present consciousness of an Absolute or of objective reality as the exemplar: though we cannot form a determinate conception of the Absolute, its persistent presence in consciousness gives it the highest validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness of the Absolute is positive (not mere negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our consciousness of the Unconditioned/Absolute is necessarily positive and not merely a negation of conceivability (contra the view that the Absolute is only 'the mere absence of the conditions under which consciousness is possible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points out apparent inconsistencies in writers (Hamilton, Mansel) who describe the Absolute as both a negation and as an inspiring positive conviction. The positive character is explained by the process of thought: successive negations of particular forms leave an indestructible, indefinite element—the raw material of consciousness—which is experienced as a positive sense of unconditioned existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indestructible belief in an inscrutable reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when philosophy proves the reality underlying appearances to be inconceivable, subjective consciousness compels a belief in a real Non-relative or Absolute which underlies relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when conceiving bounded space/time or definite causes, thought carries us to a nascent consciousness of a transcendent space/time or Cause. Although we cannot form determinate conceptions of this reality, the continual persistence of the element of 'existence' across changing modes of thought yields a firm belief in objective reality that metaphysical criticism cannot erase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion's proper function: assert mystery without illegitimate positive claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion's essential merit is the assertion and diffusion of the supreme verity—the recognition of an inscrutable Power—and its task is to awaken consciousness to something beyond the immediate; it errs when it professes definite knowledge of the transcendent or clings to untenable dogmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises religion for maintaining the fundamental intuition of mystery across history but criticizes its tendencies to (a) claim positive attributes for the inscrutable Cause, (b) maintain untenable dogmas after criticism, and (c) display a secret scepticism that leads to fear of inquiry. Proper religious posture is fidelity to the recognition of mystery while avoiding false precision about the Absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's proper function: provide positive knowledge while avoiding metaphysical reification
rubrics_metrics.description: Science, understood as positive and definite knowledge of relations among phenomena, should progressively generalize relations but must avoid treating abstract explanatory constructs as ultimate, comprehensible entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (aureity, vital principle, distinct imponderables) show science's unscientific habit of assuming ultimate knowable agents. Advanced science should regard its explanations as progressively more abstract and ultimately proximate/relative, not as claims to know the absolute nature of causes (e.g., gravitation is explanatorily powerful but its ultimate nature remains incomprehensible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate spheres to reduce conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreements between Religion and Science arise from incomplete differentiation of their proper spheres; peace requires Science to admit its explanations are proximate/relative and Religion to accept the ultimate mystery of the inscrutable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues conflicts stem from each claiming the other's territory: Religion claiming positive knowledge of the inscrutable, Science treating nescience as knowledge. As both relinquish illegitimate claims and respect respective limits, antagonism diminishes and reconciliation follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress is dual: advance toward both the natural and the supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Every intellectual advance moves both toward more general, predictive knowledge of phenomena and toward causes that are less representable in ordinary thought (thus more 'incomprehensible'), so scientific progress is simultaneously a movement toward the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by historical development (mythical agency → Kepler's animating spirits → Newtonian gravitation): increased generality yields causes less readily imagined though more predictive. This duality explains why scientific development can make beliefs more 'religious' (less concretely imaginable) even as it increases explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual purification as route to reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion and Science purify and correct each other: religion preserves the recognition of the Inscrutable while science refines and strips away incoherent dogmas; together their mutual criticisms lead to an ultimate agreement about an inscrutable reality whose existence is warranted though its nature remains unknowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter concludes that the convergence of arguments from objective (science) and subjective (philosophical) considerations yields a reconciliation: the Absolute cannot be known in content but is a necessary datum of consciousness, and both disciplines approach this conclusion from different angles and correct each other's excesses.
